modeling_assumptions.text: At-bats exclude walks (real baseball convention): AB = 1B+2B+3B+HR+Outs; PA = AB+Walks. Batting average = hits/AB. The D2 outcome-percentage breakdown uses PA as its denominator, a genuinely different quantity from AB -- stated explicitly in Appendix C because conflating them is the most likely student error.

Rounding convention: batting averages to 3 decimal places, percentages to the nearest tenth of a percent. Because of rounding, a player's 6 outcome percentages may not sum to exactly 100.0% -- disclosed in Appendix C as expected, not an error.

The case deliberately asks Carly to decide WHO is in the lineup, not WHAT ORDER they bat in -- Appendix C explains this using D5's own Fundamental Counting Principle result (362,880 possible orders for a fixed 9-player lineup) as the justification, so the scope decision is itself a worked answer, not an unexplained rule.

deliverables.text: A batting-average table for all 15 players: hits, at-bats, and batting average (hits / at-bats), rounded to 3 decimal places.
A plate-appearance outcome breakdown for all 15 players: percentage of PA resulting in a walk, single, double, triple, home run, and out, rounded to the nearest tenth of a percent.
Both lineups' overall batting performance stated two ways -- combined batting average and mean of individual averages -- with one sentence on why they differ.
One original bar graph comparing Ash's and Venicia's lineups on whichever statistic the student argues matters most.
The number of distinct batting orders possible for a fixed 9-player lineup, using the Fundamental Counting Principle, and one sentence on why the case sets ordering aside.

balance.argument_a: Ash's nine hitters post a real .514 combined batting average (218 hits / 424 at-bats) against Venicia's .475 (214/451) -- an 8.2% edge on the exact number the original Guide Notes anchors ask Heroes to compute first. Ash's lineup is built around Swensen (.630 AVG) and Jacoby (.615 AVG), the two hottest bats on the entire spring roster, and neither is on Venicia's lineup at all.
balance.argument_b: Venicia's lineup trades average for power: her nine hitters combine for 39 home runs against Ash's 24 -- 62.5% more -- and a team slugging percentage (total bases / at-bat) of .958 against Ash's .917, a 4.5% edge on the standard measure of raw power. The single most dangerous bat on either roster is Poppins (14 HR in just 72 plate appearances, a .958-pulling 1.292 individual slugging percentage nobody else on the roster approaches) -- a player Ash did not pick at all.
balance.margin_basis: On combined batting average (this case's stated primary metric) Ash leads by 8.2%, comfortably inside SPEC's 20% balance cap. On slugging percentage -- a real, equally legitimate second lens on the same Appendix A data -- Venicia leads by 4.5%. The case does not resolve which number should decide a hire; that tension is the discussion.

derived._note: Worked from Appendix A's real given data. Computed during conversion; case-readiness should re-derive independently, not just trust this block. avg_margin_pct_ash_favored and slg_margin_pct_venicia_favored are computed from the already-3-decimal-rounded AVG/SLG figures (per case.md Appendix C, Assumption 2), not from the raw unrounded ratios -- the unrounded versions are 8.36% and 4.41% respectively, about a tenth of a point off.
